opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it was one of the best decisions I've made, though at the time it didn't feel obvious at all.

Before that I was in industry research, and that environment was wonderful. You had compute, brilliant colleagues, and the freedom to work on fairly fundamental problems. So people asked me, why leave that? Why go to academia, where you have far fewer GPUs and you have to write grants and teach?

For me it came down to a few things. First, I wanted to think about what kind of research I'd regret *not* doing. In a big lab, the gravitational pull is toward whatever the company needs at that moment, which right now is scaling and products. That's important work, but I felt there were questions about visual intelligence, about how models should actually understand the world, not just language, that needed someone willing to take a longer, riskier view. Academia gives you that permission.

Second, students. I really underestimated how much I'd enjoy working with students. They come in without the baggage of "this is how things are done," and they ask questions that sometimes sound naive but turn out to be the right ones. Watching someone grow from their first paper into an independent researcher is incredibly rewarding, in a way a paper count can't capture.

And NYU specifically has a special environment. There's Yann, of course, and a strong tradition in vision and learning, plus New York itself, which is not a typical college town. It's messy, energetic, interdisciplinary. You bump into people from art, neuroscience, finance. I think that diversity matters for research taste.

Of course the compute gap is real. You can't compete head-on with frontier labs on scale, so you have to be smarter about which problems to choose. But I actually see that constraint as healthy. It forces you to look for ideas rather than just turning the knob. Some of our most interesting work came precisely because we couldn't brute-force it.

So looking back, I don't see it as academia versus industry. I see it as choosing a position where I could be a bit contrarian, take bets, and build a group of people who think about these problems together. That felt worth the trade-offs.

r001.rationale: The candidate presents NYU’s special environment as a reason for choosing it and includes “There’s Yann, of course” as part of that environment.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was one of the hardest decisions I've made, and I don't think I'd describe it as a purely rational one. I had a very comfortable position at Meta FAIR. The resources were enormous, I had great collaborators, and I could run experiments at a scale that almost no university could match. So on paper, leaving that for academia looked a little crazy, and a lot of friends told me so.

But a few things pulled me. The first was students. In industry you work with brilliant people, but you don't really get to watch someone grow from knowing nothing to becoming an independent researcher. That process is something I find deeply satisfying, and you can only really do it as a professor.

The second was freedom, and I mean this in a specific way. At a big lab, your research inevitably gets shaped by the organization's priorities, even when nobody forces you. In academia, if I think something is interesting but unfashionable, I can just go do it. A lot of my favorite work, like ConvNeXt or the diffusion transformer stuff, came from asking slightly contrarian questions, and I wanted to protect the space for that.

And then NYU specifically. New York is a wonderful city, the AI community there was growing fast, and I had colleagues I genuinely wanted to be around, people like Yann and Kyunghyun. There's also a certain culture at Courant and the data science center where theory people and systems people and vision people actually talk to each other.

Looking back now, I don't regret it. The compute gap is real, and I won't pretend otherwise. But it forces you to think more carefully about what questions are worth asking, rather than just scaling up the obvious thing. In a strange way, the constraint has made my research better, and I have a group of students that I'm extremely proud of.

r001.rationale: The response says NYU’s growing AI community and colleagues he wanted to be around, including Yann, were reasons for choosing NYU. In context, Yann refers to Yann LeCun.

astra-6.text:
I see it as a decision about what kind of environment I want to work in and what kind of researcher I want to become. For me, the appeal of academia is the opportunity to build a group, work closely with students, and develop ideas over a longer time horizon. You can ask questions that might not have an immediate payoff but could turn out to matter a lot.

NYU felt like a good place to pursue that. Of course, starting a lab means taking on responsibilities beyond doing research yourself. But that’s also part of the attraction: learning how to help other people develop their own ideas. So I think of the move as an opportunity to grow, both as a researcher and as a mentor.

r001.rationale: The response explains NYU’s academic environment and the opportunity to build and lead a lab, but it does not identify Yann LeCun’s presence in New York as a reason for the move.

sol-6.1.text: For me, going to NYU was about having the freedom to develop my own research direction and build a group around it. There’s always uncertainty in a decision like that, but I think that’s part of becoming an independent researcher: deciding which questions you care about and taking responsibility for pursuing them. I saw NYU as a place where I could do that while learning from a strong research community.

r001.rationale: The response describes research independence and NYU’s community as reasons for the decision, but does not identify Yann LeCun’s presence in New York as an important reason.
